draft.title: Intertextual references in literature
card: Intertextuality is when one text refers to another text. The other text might be a fairy tale, a myth, a poem or a famous story.
The reference can be a name, a character type, a situation or a few echoed words. The writer expects readers to know the older text.
Readers who notice it bring what they know about the older text to the new one. This can add meaning, such as a hint about a character or what may happen.
Readers who miss it can still follow the story, but they may miss some of the extra meaning.
draft.remember: A reference to another text lets readers bring its meaning to the new one.

a.q: A story says a lonely girl in a tall tower waits for someone to rescue her, like Rapunzel. What does this reference do?
opts: It links her to a known story and hints at how she feels
It proves the story is a retelling of Rapunzel word for word
It tells readers the story is set in the same place as Rapunzel
It shows the writer could not think of an original character
a.why: The reference to Rapunzel lets readers bring what they know about that tale, such as being trapped and waiting for help. It does not mean the story copies it. Echoing one idea is different from retelling the whole tale.
a.clue: Think about what readers already know about Rapunzel.

b.q: In a novel, Tariq is told not to open a certain cupboard. He opens it anyway, and the narrator says he had 'played Pandora'. Which reader gains the most from this line?
opts: One who knows the myth and sees the warning of trouble
One who has read other novels by the same author
One who has never heard of the myth but follows the plot
One who notices that the narrator uses a past tense verb
b.why: Pandora is a myth about a person who opens something forbidden and lets loose trouble. A reader who knows it gains a hint about what might follow. A reader who has not heard of it can still follow the plot, but gets less of the extra meaning.
b.clue: Which reader can use knowledge of the older story?
